newsitem.title: INDIA: India Reliance profits up, seen soaring in 1997/98.
newsitem.headline: India Reliance profits up, seen soaring in 1997/98.

text.p: Indian petrochemicals giant Reliance Industries Ltd on Tuesday announced modestly higher profit for 1996/97 (April-March) and analysts said they expect robust earnings in the current year.
Net profit rose to 13.23 billion rupees from 13.05 billion in 1995/96 on higher sales of 87.3 billion rupees against 77.86 billion a year ago.
"This is a pleasant surprise," said Jal Irani, Reliance analyst at Jardine Fleming Broking India. "The reasons are two-fold -- higher than anticipated turnover and lower taxes."
A Reuter poll of leading securities and brokerage houses had estimated the firm's net profit at 12.06 billion rupees.
On the Bombay Stock Exchange, Reliance shares ended 0.25 rupees higher at 308, off a high of 320.25 -- and after rising 19 percent in the last one week.
Reliance had commissioned huge capacities for several products in the last quarter of fiscal 1996/97 and better utilisations may have resulted in the higher sales, he said.

These included 360,000 tonnes a year polypropylene plant, 120,000 tonne mono ethylene glycol, 350,000 tonne purified terephthalic acid, 160,000 tonne polyester staple fibre and 60,000 tonne polyester fibre -- all raw materials that go into the manufacture of textiles or plastics.
Reliance, India's largest private firm, provided a measly 450 million rupees for taxes.
"The tax outgo is the biggest surprise," said another analyst at an European securities firm. "This works out to 3.3 percent on profits against the 12.9 percent MAT (minimum alternate tax)."
The lower taxes may be because of tax breaks on projects in undeveloped remote areas, he said.
Reliance had avoided paying taxes since it went public in 1977 by ploughing back profits into tax-spared expansions and diversifications.

Some analysts believe the profits may have also been helped by interest costs of 1.7 billion rupees, though the firm's gross block jumped 59 percent to 109.56 billion rupees from 68.86 billion in 1995/96.
"The interest charges were 34 percent lower than our estimates," the European securities firm analyst said. "This could be due to capitalisation of interest."
Companies normally capitalise interest by adding the charge to the cost of machinery or building. This results in pushing profits up and enables companies to write off higher depreciation.
Full benefit from new production capacity would be felt only in fiscal 1997/98 and analysts are bullish on Reliance. They expect profits to rise sharply on huge volume growth.
Reliance started a new 750,000 tonnes a year ethylene facility at its Hazira plant on the west coast which can also produce 2.2 million tonnes of several byproducts.
"The cracker has gone on stream at the right time," said Jardine's Irani. "Ethylene prices have risen to $700 a tonne from $500 over the past eight months."
The company has said the project would insulate it from dependence on world markets and boost margins.

By the end of 1997/98, volume output is expected to rise to 6.2 million tonnes from 1.6 million tonnes in 1995/96, and expansion projects on hand would take the total capacity to 9.3 million tonnes by 1998/99, analysts said.
"The outlook is very good," said Ajay Jindal, analyst at Caspian Securities. "Sales volume would grow 70 percent in fiscal 1997/98. In value terms it should be up 40 percent."
Reliance is expected to weather adverse market conditions by its access to economies of scale, analysts said.
Estimates on net profit range from 16 billion rupees to 20 billion rupees for 1997/98.
